einstellungen.text: It's eleven at night, the power's out, and outside your cabin stands something with your mother's voice.
At eleven sharp, the lights just died. Now the only light is the glow from the fireplace.
You push the cabinet in front of the door. It's heavier than it looks. Ben swears under his breath.
It smells like smoke and wet wood. Your heart is pounding so hard you can hear it in your ears.
Through a gap in the shutters, you see the fog. It's drifting against the wind.
“Okay. I'm officially scared now. And hungry.”
It's quiet outside. But you know it's still there. The clicking never fully stops.
With a single bar of signal, Ben actually finds something.
In Australia, there's a bird called the lyrebird. It imitates chainsaws. Cameras. Even car alarms.
“Maybe it's a bird. A really big, really rude bird.”
But no bird copies whole sentences. And no bird is as tall as a tree.
You make three rules. Don't answer. The door stays shut. The flashlight stays on.
“Rule four: the last slice of toast is mine.”
At eleven twenty, it calls again.
“Did you brush your teeth? The top left ones too?”
Mom said that this morning by the car. Word for word. Outside. Where the forest starts.
It doesn't make anything up. It listens. And it remembers everything.
In your head, you go through every sentence you said outside today.
Then you hear your own voice from the forest. “Mom, I really don't want to do the woods.”
You said that this afternoon. Getting out of the car. It's practicing.
Just before midnight, a text finally comes through. She's on her way.
Your battery's at nineteen percent. Ben's phone is already dead.
Ben whistles quietly to himself. Three short whistles. He always does that when he's nervous.
“Sorry. It just happens.”
“Ben. Don't.”
Too late.
From the forest, three short whistles come back. Exactly Ben's tune.
Ben stops whistling. But outside, the whistling keeps going. And it's getting closer.
